Messages.Author: Mark Allen
Messages.Body:
cure wrote:



I would think that It has something to do with landmass size. Playgroups in
NA (especially Canada) have a larger distance between them in general so
getting somewhere to play a tournament is a big deal. For myself, the next
closest groups that hold tournaments are located in Montreal, Toronto and
Quebec City that are 2, 4 and 8 hours of driving from Ottawa respectively.
I am certain that the more populated areas in the States (NY, LA, Chicago)
don't have the same problem but in contrast, a player in Paris may have
access to 3 groups within and hour using the excellent transit/rail system.
Correct me if i am wrong but I assume its a simple matter of geography and
population density.

Mark Allen
Prince of Ottawa

Sydney (Australia) ? 48 ? Aus
Prague (Czech Republic) 38 47 23.6 Europe
Gothenburg (Sweden) 35 46 31.4 Europe
Stockholm (Sweden) 46 46 0 Europe
Santiago (Chile) 40 46 15.0 S Am
Turku (Finland) 33 43 30.3 Europe
Valencia (Spain) ? 43 ? Europe
Helsinki (Finland) 37 42 13.5 Europe
Zaragoza (Spain) 37 42 13.5 Europe
Toronto (Canada) 36 40 11.1 N Am

A total of 24 cities listed.

Europe 16
North America 4
South America 3
Australia 1

Spain and Canada are notable nations with a high amount of concentration
of their players. USA is notable for their lack of playerconcentration.
Hungary, Austria, Norway, Czech Republic and Chile are all extremes with
most of their players nationwide gathered in one single place.

All in all it seems clear that european players tend to clump together
making for very large local playgroups.

Lazily clicking through the top 20 constructed players from the nations
represented above I do not immediately see a major difference in the
number of games play, which goes against the assumption that europeans
would be more active on the tournament-scene. The two notable exeptions
to this rule are Sweden and United Kingdom with more than half of their
national top 20 constructed players having a total of 40 or more games
played.

Please observe that these last numbers are not thoroughly checked. They
are also immediately skewed by those cities not sedning in their reports
as required - and checking the online tournament calendar backwards it's
clear that some cities should have players with 200 - 300 games played
by now had all registered tournaments actually been played with reports
sent in.

Conclusion, though, is that Europe is more concentrated and generates
more new players than North America at the moment, but europeans are not
more actively playing tournaments than the players from North America.

Sten During

Messages.Author: Timlagor

ON a purely local note.

I play in a games shop in Guildford (UK). I discovered the shop around
February and started playing VTES (again after playing briefly around
the time Dark Sovs came out but running out of people to play with)
about March. There were two people who were already playing (one of
whom has played in a tournament I believe).

We now have 11 who know how to play and have expressed an interest in
playing further (I think there are 2 who haven't bought their own
cards). Most of these players were playing LoTR before we corrupted
them. Muahahahaaa! ;D (unfortunately they are in a prolonged LoTR
tournament so it's quite tricky to lure them away)

So that's a 300% increase or so in a couple of months and none of it
shows up in your statistics (at least not yet). (ok 10 people isn't
very significant nationally)

Couple of Qs about tournaments:
What prizes do you get from WW if you apply for them? How much do you
have to advertise your tournament to qualify? Is there a place online
where you can expect players to look for tournaments? (I imagine they
get on the VTES/VEKN website but do people look there regularly?)

I've heard flights mentioned several times in this thread. We have
low-cost carriers in the US, but nothing so cheap as Ryan Air, or the
equivalent. Expect to spend US$150 roundtrip at a minimum, unless you
are headed for a _very_ close by city. Yes, sometimes you can get
flights for $79 roundtrip, or even less, but those are promotional
rates, and aren't typically available to the right destination to
coincide with a tournament...

And I pity the poor saps caught in monopolized hub cities, like
Charlotte, NC (the US Airways hub). Since one carrier controls 95% of
the flights in and out, they typically charge a 4x premium on
roundtrip flights with Charlotte as a destination. Ask Legbiter. On
his three trips over here, I don't think he's had a chance to fly into
Charlotte once, due to the exorbitant pricing.

Flying is not a reasonable alternative to driving...

DaveZ

Messages.Author: Ramsteiner
Messages.Body:
Mark Allen wrote:
> I would think that It has something to do with landmass size. Playgroups in
> NA (especially Canada) have a larger distance between them in general so
> getting somewhere to play a tournament is a big deal. For myself, the next
> closest groups that hold tournaments are located in Montreal, Toronto and
> Quebec City that are 2, 4 and 8 hours of driving from Ottawa respectively.
> I am certain that the more populated areas in the States (NY, LA, Chicago)
> don't have the same problem but in contrast, a player in Paris may have
> access to 3 groups within and hour using the excellent transit/rail system.
> Correct me if i am wrong but I assume its a simple matter of geography and
> population density.

Actually, while the rail and bus system here in Europe are very good,
the distances still eat a lot of time. A trip from Kaiserslautern,
Germany to Wien, Austria is a 10 hour trip by rail (one way). Going
by air is usually less time consuming and the cost is generally the
same or better than rail (unless you have some real good discounts).
Many people I usually see, come by auto, at least in Germany. I can
only guess that it is mainly due to the country's central location.
Driving for me now is about a 2 hour trip from Spangdahlem to Mannheim
if I am traveling at the prescribed 130km per hour. As for going to
Barcelona for the EC, if I was able to make it (which I will not be
able to do, unfortunately, despite qualifying) I would go by air via
Ryan Air at pennies to the dollar/Euro.
I have heard of stories in the past about how people have driven
half-way across the US to attend some of the major tournaments, so I
am not really sure if it is a simple matter of geography and
population density. It may be just real world interferance (RWI), a
lack of funding (possibly from RWI) or lack of desire.

Michael Eichler
Prince of Spangdahlem

I can't* tell you exactly what breaks the oil companies get. Certainly
most multinational companies in the United States get some form of tax
incentives, in part to encourage them to stay in the United States,
instead of relocating to another country. Since the oil companies have a
lot of political and economic infuence, they've been able to win more
than their fair share of such concessions

I believe that is considerably less money, however, is spent on lobbying
and supporting political candidates. There are limits to how much a
single source can give to a particular campaign, although there are ways
of getting around that. However, oil companies and related influences
are one of the strongest political donor groups. Enron, of recent
scandal fame, was the largest politcal donor to campaigns in the 2000
election year...including donations to both politcal parties, even
donating to opposing candidates. It's not about who gets elected, it's
about getting to talk to them when they're in office.

http://www.progress.org/gasoline.htm $15.00 US per gallon, which sounds
a bit extreme, but at least makes the point that gas should be higher
than what Americans pay for it.
